The exact timestamp of the alert trigger was not specified in the available information.", "startedAt": "2026-10-02T15:18:36.327738+00:00", "analyzedAt": null, "resolvedAt": null, "sourceType": "chat"}, {"id": "b6e5638e-d926-4ce3-8341-4366d137ecb2", "status": "analyzed", "severity": "high", "title": "HighErrorRate", "service": "shop", "environment": null, "auroraStatus": "complete", "summary": "## Incident Report

**What Happened**

At 2026-10-02T15:13:44, a HighErrorRate alert was triggered for the `shop` service. Frontend nginx logs show continuous 502 responses for `/api/items` and other `/api/*` requests, with errors recurring on every load-generator request from 15:13:01 onward, including a live example at 15:14:11 referencing connection refused errors to upstream `10.96.35.67:8080` [7]. At the time of the alert, all pods in the `shop` namespace — including both `api` pods and both `frontend` pods — were reporting `Running` with zero restarts [5, 14].

**Root Cause**

The root cause was a selector mismatch on the `api` Service in the `shop` namespace. The Service's live selector was `app=api-v2` [10, 12], but both running `api` pods carry the label `app=api`, and no pod anywhere in the cluster carries the label `app=api-v2` [13, 14, 17]. As a result, the Service had zero endpoints [11], causing kube-proxy to refuse all connections to the ClusterIP and producing the 502 errors seen in the frontend nginx logs [7]. The Service's `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation confirms it was originally applied with selector `app: api`, matching the Deployment's pod template label [15, 16], indicating the live selector was changed via an untracked edit after initial deployment rather than being the intended configuration.

**Impact & Timeline**

All `/api/*` traffic proxied through the frontend was affected from at least 15:13:01 through the time of alert triggering and evidence collection, with 502 errors returned on every request [7]. The `frontend` and `redis` Services retained healthy endpoints throughout [11], confirming the outage was isolated to the `api` Service's routing path rather than a broader namespace failure.

## Ruled Out
- Pod crash or OOM — all `api` and `frontend` pods show `RESTARTS: 0` and `STATUS: Running` [5, 14]
- nginx configuration error on frontend — ConfigMap present and nginx startup/access logs show clean operation aside from the 502 upstream errors tied to the missing endpoints [7, 9]
- api application bug — `/healthz` endpoint returns 200 consistently inside the pod, and app logs are clean apart from a transient initial redis-connect retry that succeeded [8]
- Redis connectivity issue — initial connection failure was transient and resolved on retry, with no recurring errors [8]

## Not Checked
- Deployment rollout history for the `api` Deployment was not retrievable (`kubectl rollout history` blocked by mutating-kubectl policy) [18], so the exact timing/actor of the selector edit could not be confirmed
- Audit logs or RBAC records identifying who performed the live `kubectl patch/edit` on the Service selector were not available in the evidence collected", "startedAt": "2026-10-02T15:13:44.671982+00:00", "analyzedAt": "2026-10-02T15:15:50.340047+00:00", "resolvedAt": null, "sourceType": "chat"}, {"id": "a28a7b3f-b10d-4590-bbf0-b0883532e594", "status": "analyzed", "severity": "high", "title": "KubePodCrashLooping", "service": "shop", "environment": null, "auroraStatus": "complete", "summary": "## Incident Report

**What Happened**

At 2026-10-02T15:08:06 UTC, a high-severity "KubePodCrashLooping" alert fired for the shop/api service. At the time of investigation, both api replicas (api-c7b987b4d-d8vj8 and api-c7b987b4d-wtmf8) were in a Running/Ready (1/1, 2/2) state but actively restarting on a roughly 60–70 second cadence, with Restart Count climbing (1–2 restarts within 2–3.5 minutes of pod age) [4, 7, 13]. "Killing" events for the api container were logged within 30–40 seconds of the investigation [6, 7, 13]. No other workloads in the namespace (frontend, worker, redis, loadgen) showed restarts, and all three cluster nodes were Ready [5, 12].

**Root Cause**

The root cause is confirmed. The live `api` Deployment specification has `livenessProbe.httpGet.port` set to 8081, while the `readinessProbe` correctly targets port 8080 [7, 8, 13]. The application code in the `api-code` ConfigMap binds `ThreadingHTTPServer(("", PORT), H)` with `PORT` defaulting to 8080, and no `PORT` environment override is set in the pod spec [9]. As a result, every liveness check to port 8081 receives a connection refused, and kubelet repeatedly kills and restarts the container (exit code 137) once the probe's failure threshold is reached — exactly matching the observed ~60-70s restart pattern [7, 13]. The Deployment's `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation shows the originally applied/reviewed liveness port was 8080, matching the readiness probe and the app's actual listening port [8], indicating the live object's port value was changed to 8081 outside of a tracked `kubectl apply`.

**Impact & Timeline**

Pods for api started around 15:06 UTC, with the alert triggering at 15:08:06 UTC after restarts began accumulating [4, 7, 13]. Impact was isolated to the two api replicas; readiness checks on port 8080 continued to succeed throughout, so the service was not fully down but was cycling under repeated container kills [7, 13]. No other services in the shop namespace were affected [5, 6].

## Ruled Out
- OOMKill as the restart cause — container `Last State` shows `Terminated, Reason: Error`, not OOMKilled, and memory usage remained under the 128Mi limit with no OOM events in pod describe or namespace events [7, 13, 6].
- Recurrence of the prior log-shipper sidecar OOM incident (e68e36c8) — that sidecar container does not exist in the current single-container api pod spec [7, 13, 2].
- Node or cluster resource pressure — all three nodes report Ready status [12].
- Application or Redis-level failure — readiness probe on port 8080 succeeds (`Ready: True`); only the misdirected port-8081 liveness probe fails [7, 13, 9].
- Broader namespace impact — frontend, worker, redis, and loadgen deployments show 0 restarts and remain healthy [5, 6].

## Not Checked
- Resource usage metrics via `kubectl top pods` — Metrics API was not available in this cluster, so memory/CPU consumption could not be directly measured [11].
- Identity/timing of who or what process changed the live liveness probe port from 8080 to 8081 — no audit log or change-tracking data was available beyond the last-applied-configuration diff [8].
- Revision 1 ReplicaSet (`api-f64486c4c`) probe configuration — referenced as a comparison point but its full spec was not retrieved in this evidence set [10].", "startedAt": "2026-10-02T15:08:06.020153+00:00", "analyzedAt": "2026-10-02T15:10:42.879876+00:00", "resolvedAt": null, "sourceType": "chat"}, {"id": "6da158a5-b061-4094-ae30-7bea0f31332f", "status": "analyzed", "severity": "high", "title": "KubePodCrashLooping", "service": "shop", "environment": null, "auroraStatus": "complete", "summary": "## Incident Report

**What Happened**

At 2026-10-02T15:01:03Z, a high-severity KubePodCrashLooping alert fired for the `shop` service. Investigation of the live cluster found pod `frontend-d6db5d589-dn4kr` (part of the Deployment `frontend`) in CrashLoopBackOff status with 3 restarts, last terminated with Exit Code 1 [4, 7]. The Deployment showed READY 2/2, AVAILABLE 2, UP-TO-DATE 1/2, indicating only the newest pod was affected while the Deployment overall remained healthy [5, 8].

**Root Cause**

The root cause was a syntax error in the `frontend-nginx` ConfigMap: the directive `proxy_conect_timeout` (missing the "n" in "connect") is invalid, causing nginx to fail config validation at startup with `unknown directive "proxy_conect_timeout" in /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:9` [6, 9]. This typo is present in the ConfigMap's `last-applied-configuration` annotation, indicating it was introduced via a deliberate `kubectl apply` rather than a live edit [9]. A `kubectl rollout restart` was issued at 15:00:12 UTC, per the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` annotation on the pod template, creating a new ReplicaSet (`frontend-d6db5d589`) whose pods read the already-broken ConfigMap on startup and failed immediately [7, 13]. The older ReplicaSet (`frontend-76d98597b9`) pods were already running prior to this and had the config loaded into their nginx master process in memory, so they never re-parsed the file and continued serving traffic normally, as shown by continuous 200 OK responses in their access logs [8, 12]. The timing of the restart annotation, pod creation, and first crash align closely, consistent with this causal chain [7, 13].

**Impact & Timeline**

This is a stuck rolling update rather than a full outage: the two old-revision pods remained healthy and serving all traffic (READY 2/2, AVAILABLE 2) while the single new-revision pod repeatedly crashed [5, 8, 12]. No correlated alerts or downstream service impact were identified [14, 15].

## Ruled Out
- OOM/memory limit exceeded — no OOMKilled events observed, and the container never reached a point to consume memory since it fails at config validation before binding to port 80 [6, 7].
- Image pull failure — the image `nginx:1.27-alpine` was already present and successfully used across both ReplicaSets [5, 8].

tool_input.title: shop/worker KubePodNotReady - CPU request drift (50m -> 64 cores)
tool_input.content:
## Incident
KubePodNotReady alert: shop/worker new ReplicaSet pod (revision 2, e.g. worker-7fdf4ffb67-xxxx) stuck `Pending`, `Node: <none>`, `PodScheduled: False` for >5 min. Old revision-1 worker pod stayed Running/Ready throughout (not a full outage, just failed rollout of new replica).

## Root Cause
Live `worker` Deployment spec had `spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu` set to `"64"` (64 **whole CPU cores**) instead of `"50m"` (50 millicores). The `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation on the same Deployment still showed `"50m"`, and the still-healthy revision-1 pod's actual resource request was confirmed as `50m` — proving this was an untracked live edit/drift, not a reviewed `kubectl apply` or Deployment YAML change.

Cluster nodes (`aurora-lab-worker`, `aurora-lab-worker2`) each have only 10 allocatable CPUs; `aurora-lab-control-plane` is tainted NoSchedule (normal/expected, unrelated). A request of 64 cores can never be satisfied by any node, so the scheduler permanently rejects the pod: `FailedScheduling: 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu.`

## How to Diagnose Fast
1. `kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide` — identify the Pending pod, confirm `Node: <none>`.
2. `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n shop` — check `Events: FailedScheduling` reason text (Insufficient cpu/memory vs taint vs affinity).
3. Compare `resources.requests` in `kubectl get deployment <name> -n shop -o yaml` spec vs the `last-applied-configuration` annotation — a mismatch confirms live-edit drift (recurring org pattern in shop namespace).
4. Confirm node allocatable capacity with `kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.allocatable.cpu}'` to quantify how far off the request is.

## Fix (requires write access — blocked under read-only policy)
`kubectl patch deployment worker -n shop --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu","value":"50m"}]'`
Low risk — reverts to the known-good, previously-applied value also present on the still-running revision-1 pod.

## Pattern Note
This is the 9th distinct root-cause mechanism identified in the shop namespace's recurring "untracked live-edit drift" incident family (see also: liveness probe port 8081 vs 8080, Service selector app=api-v2, missing DB_PASSWORD Secret, frontend image tag typo, nginx ConfigMap proxy_conect_timeout typo, log-shipper sidecar OOM, worker BATCH_SIZE OOM). Common thread: `last-applied-configuration` annotation retains the correct/reviewed value while the live object has been hand-edited to an incorrect one — always diff these two before trusting the live spec.
tool_input.description: shop/worker pod stuck Pending (KubePodNotReady) because live Deployment spec had resources.requests.cpu drifted from 50m to 64 (whole cores, not millicores) via untracked live edit, exceeding each node's 10-core allocatable capacity -> FailedScheduling/Insufficient cpu. 9th distinct shop-namespace root-cause mechanism.
